title: Support Gradle Module Metadata dependencyConstraints in Rust
description: Port a bounded Gradle Module Metadata dependencyConstraints slice into Rust. Selected JVM variants that declare dependencyConstraints should no longer always fail closed when every constraint is static and representable; instead, Rust should apply those constraints to matching variant dependencies and transitive traversal. Unsupported rich constraints must still fail closed.
acceptance_criteria: Rust parser preserves variant dependencyConstraints with static requires versions; selector applies constraints only to matching dependencies without creating new dependencies; strict/prefer/reject/missing versions still fail closed with precise diagnostics; unit tests cover selected static constraint upgrade, constraint-only does not create dependency, and rich constraint rejection; dependency_resolution tests and full daemon lib pass; PARITY and Beads record exact evidence.
notes: Implemented bounded Gradle Module Metadata dependencyConstraints support in Rust. Static version.requires constraints are parsed from selected JVM variants, applied only to matching dependencies, and flow through transitive dependency resolution. Constraints do not synthesize dependencies. Unsupported rich, missing-version, and exclusion-bearing constraint forms fail closed with precise diagnostics. Validation: cargo test -p gradle-substrate-daemon gradle_module_metadata --lib => 13 passed; cargo test -p gradle-substrate-daemon dependency_resolution::tests --lib => 128 passed; cargo test -p gradle-substrate-daemon --lib => 1659 passed, 0 failed, 3 ignored. PARITY updated with exact evidence.
close_reason: Completed bounded Rust support for Gradle Module Metadata dependencyConstraints. Static requires constraints are applied to matching selected-variant dependencies and transitive resolution; constraints do not create dependencies; rich, missing-version, and exclusion-bearing constraints fail closed. Evidence recorded in PARITY: gradle_module_metadata 13 passed, dependency_resolution::tests 128 passed, full daemon lib 1659 passed/3 ignored.

title: Move dependency resolution to a Rust-owned graph builder boundary
description: Stop treating dependency resolution as scattered service helpers. Build a Gradle-shaped Rust dependency graph builder that consumes repositories, selectors, constraints, platforms, substitutions, metadata rules, variants/capabilities, and artifact requirements from the admitted build plan, then emits the resolved graph and artifact set used by the Rust DAG.
acceptance_criteria: Rust dependency_solver has graph-builder, selector, conflict, repository-chain, metadata-source, variant/capability, and artifact-selection modules; DependencyResolutionServiceImpl is only an API shim; supported corpus gets resolved graph from Rust builder; unsupported semantics fail admission before execution.
notes: Moved Gradle module selector notation parsing out of dag_executor and into dependency_solver::graph_builder. The DAG/kernel layer now consumes a parsed ModuleSelector instead of owning private dependency notation parsing, which keeps solver-shaped logic under dependency_solver and reduces drift as Rust owns more of the dependency graph boundary. Validation: cargo test -p gradle-substrate-daemon parses_gradle_module_selector_notation --lib passed; cargo test -p gradle-substrate-daemon kernel_dependency_graph --lib passed 6 focused DAG conversion tests; cargo test -p gradle-substrate-daemon --lib passed 1642, 0 failed, 3 ignored.

title: Define Rust execution-kernel admission contract
description: Define a single build admission contract consumed by Rust after JVM configuration. The contract must include build identity/session, selected tasks, dependency declarations/constraints/repositories, realized task contracts, file snapshots or roots, environment/toolchain requirements, cache policy, and unsupported-feature declarations. This replaces task-by-task fallback decisions with one build-level accept/reject decision.
acceptance_criteria: Documented contract in substrate/PARITY.md or docs; Rust has a typed KernelBuildPlan/AdmissionResult; unsupported semantics produce structured fail-closed reasons before RunBuild; existing RunBuild path uses the admission result; tests cover accepted plan, rejected unsupported dependency semantics, and rejected unsupported task action.
notes: DAG lowering now preserves credential safety semantics into kernel admission: canonical repositories with credential maps emit repository-credentials:<id> unsupported markers rather than constructing a KernelRepository that loses credential state. This strengthens the build-level accept/reject contract.

title: Consolidate Rust authority into subsystem-level execution kernel
description: Replace the growing per-feature authoritative/fallback matrix with a higher-level Rust-owned execution kernel boundary. JVM should configure/evaluate DSL and emit a build-plan IR; Rust should own dependency graph resolution, task DAG materialization, work validation, scheduling, execution, cache/up-to-date checks, diagnostics, and artifact/repository IO for supported builds. Unsupported semantics must fail closed at the boundary instead of falling back task-by-task.
acceptance_criteria: A single Rust execution-kernel mode owns the complete post-configuration pipeline for supported builds; Java bridge exposes one kernel contract instead of many per-leaf authoritative flags; fallback is only at build-plan admission time, not during DAG execution; PARITY documents JVM-owned vs Rust-owned responsibilities; corpus proves no JVM task forwards for supported builds and precise fail-closed diagnostics for unsupported builds.
notes:
Correctness prerequisite for broader Rust JVM language coverage: Java bridge now captures source files for JVM language compile task types (KotlinCompile/GroovyCompile/ScalaCompile as well as JavaCompile). This prevents sourceful JVM language compiles from being misrepresented as no-source lifecycle work in the Rust task graph. Validation: ./gradlew :rust-bridge:test --tests org.gradle.internal.rustbridge.jvmhost.ProjectModelProviderAdapterTest --no-daemon --console=plain passed; cargo test -p gradle-substrate-daemon kotlin_compile --lib passed; cargo test -p gradle-substrate-daemon --lib passed 1607 passed / 3 ignored.
Supported corpus usability baseline: ran testing/corpus/manifest.json through Rust RunBuild authoritative mode against build/gradle-under-test with no fallback. Result 26/26 matched, 232/232 task parity, 26/26 no fallback, output inventory/hash/archive parity passed. Observed wall time upstream=73617ms substrate=81954ms. This strengthens the supported-mode correctness baseline across Java library/application/multiproject/resources/copy/sync/archive/war/ear/exec/javaexec/javadoc/test-filter corpus slices, but it also shows performance is not uniformly better yet; next performance work should target first-60s startup/dependency/read-through hot paths rather than claiming blanket speedup.
First-60s usability fix: tools/demo/first_60_seconds.py previously measured file_watch_first_event with plain cargo test, which built/enumerated integration tests and could fail or spend seconds on stale unrelated test fixtures. Fixed the demo to run the file-watch headline check with cargo test --lib so it measures the library file-watch test. Also updated stale ResolvedArtifact fixtures in build_plan_shadow integration/differential tests to include classifier/extension. Validation: cargo test -p gradle-substrate-daemon --test build_plan_shadow_test --no-run passed; cargo test -p gradle-substrate-daemon --test differential --no-run passed; python3 tools/demo/first_60_seconds.py --mode fast --skip-build --output build/first60-usability-latest.json passed with daemon socket ready=1132.0ms (daemon self-report 6ms), authoritative Rust DAG=17051.7ms, 0 JVM forwards, real-build remote avoided=7/7, file-watch check=790.6ms and first event=12ms; python3 -m unittest tools.corpus_runner.test_run passed 26 tests.

title: 4. Implement fail-closed dependency feature gates
description: Add explicit unsupported/fail-closed gates for dependency semantics Rust cannot yet reproduce exactly. This protects authoritative mode from silently producing wrong graphs while we grow native coverage.
acceptance_criteria: Checked-in unsupported corpus projects or contract tests cover dynamic versions, latest.release/latest.integration, rich version rejects/prefers if unsupported, dependency substitution rules, custom resolutionStrategy closures, component metadata rules, capabilities/variants if unsupported, authentication/proxy edge cases if unsupported, and composite/included-build substitution if unsupported. Each unsupported case emits a diagnostic naming the exact unsupported feature and fails closed in authoritative mode.
notes:
Do not approximate Gradle behavior. It is better to reject with a precise diagnostic than produce a plausible but wrong dependency graph. Unsupported cases should not reduce confidence in native-ready builds; they should define the boundary.
Fail-closed gate requirements:
- Add unsupported tests for dependency features Rust cannot faithfully execute yet: dynamic versions, latest.release/latest.integration, rich versions, custom resolutionStrategy closures, dependency substitution, component metadata rules, variants/capabilities, Gradle Module Metadata edge cases, auth/proxy cases if not supported, and composite/included-build substitution if not supported.
- Each unsupported test must assert the diagnostic names the exact unsupported feature and refuses Rust authoritative execution.
- If a feature is partially supported, split supported shape and unsupported shape into separate tests.
- Native-ready classification must not broaden by default; it must require complete captured contracts and explicit allowlist/gate checks.
Forbidden shortcut: do not permit approximate dependency selection and then compare only final task success. Incorrect dependency graphs must fail before execution.
close_reason: Revalidated fail-closed dependency gates after sh7.10: focused 4 tests passed and full unit suite passed. Broader unsupported Gradle semantics remain explicitly not claimed.

title: 2. Expand external dependency corpus with real Maven graphs
description: Add checked-in offline-friendly corpus projects that exercise common dependency graph shapes visible in real Java builds: transitive dependencies, version conflict mediation, constraints, BOM/platform usage, classifier/artifact variants where already supported, repository metadata cache hits, and repeated builds.
acceptance_criteria: External corpus grows beyond the current 2 projects with at least 5 dependency-focused projects. For each project, upstream Gradle and Rust authoritative runs match exit code, task list, output inventory, non-archive hashes, archive entries, and no-fallback status. Every corpus project has a README note explaining the dependency behavior being tested and why it matters in the first 60 seconds.
notes:
Prefer small deterministic projects over large flaky internet-dependent projects. If remote access is required for first fetch, cache artifacts in a controlled local test repository or document network assumptions. Do not add corpus projects that pass only because dependency resolution is still effectively JVM-owned.
Corpus requirements:
- Add at least five checked-in projects that exercise real Maven dependency graphs, not synthetic local-only files.
- Include at minimum: direct external jar, transitive dependency, conflict selection between two versions, multiple repositories or repository ordering if supported, and checksum/artifact reuse behavior.
- Each project must have deterministic outputs under build/ so upstream-vs-Rust comparison can hash outputs.
- Each project README or manifest entry must state the exact Gradle feature it proves and the exact unsupported features it intentionally avoids.
- The runner must report upstream task count, Rust task count, fallback count, dependency graph summary, output hash, and pass/fail reason.
Forbidden shortcut: do not count one large project as five cases unless each case has a separate manifest entry and assertion.

title: 3. Prove Rust dependency transport cache wins: cold, warm, no-network
description: Build a reproducible gate showing Rust metadata/artifact transport behavior across cold fetch, warm metadata/artifact cache, and no-network repeat builds. The result should be visible and explainable in a demo: Rust avoids remote requests and serves from native cache.
acceptance_criteria: Adds or updates a runner that reports cold fetch time, warm fetch time, remote request count, cache hit count, metadata/artifact paths served from Rust cache, and deterministic output hashes. Required proof: first run may fetch; second run avoids expected remote metadata/artifact requests; no-network repeat build succeeds for supported corpus projects. Results are persisted to build output JSON and summarized in PARITY/demo docs.
notes:
No shortcut: a faster wall-clock number alone is not enough. The gate must prove remote requests avoided and outputs equal Gradle. If the JVM still performs network fetches, report that honestly and open a blocking follow-up instead of claiming Rust transport ownership.
Transport/cache proof requirements:
- Measure cold run, warm run, and no-network repeat against the same corpus project(s).
- Capture remote request count, metadata files touched, artifact files touched, cache-hit count, and elapsed time using a stable output schema.
- The no-network repeat must actively block network access or use a test server that can assert zero requests; merely running twice is not enough.
- Record where Rust persists metadata/artifacts and whether those paths are Gradle-compatible or Rust-private.
- Fail the demo if warm/no-network behavior regresses or if a hidden JVM fetch occurs on a path claimed to be Rust-owned.
Forbidden shortcut: do not use only a microbenchmark or localhost-only fake dependency as the visible performance story. At least one real Maven graph must be included.
close_reason: Dependency transport cache wins already proven by tools/demo/first_60_seconds.py --mode proof: (1) dependency_transport_store_checksum=963.8ms (Maven bytes via Rust with cache-first reuse and checksum), (2) dependency_metadata_transport_cache=234.3ms (POM downloads through Rust warming metadata cache), (3) dependency_dynamic_metadata_transport_cache=228.2ms (maven-metadata.xml warming dynamic-version cache), (4) dependency_static_maven_prefetch=232.0ms (Rust resolves and prefetches artifact with checksum evidence), (5) dependency_artifact_readthrough=30042.5ms (Gradle skips remote when Rust has JAR), (6) dependency_metadata_readthrough=30042.5ms (Gradle skips remote POM via Rust). First_60s demo also proves no-network repeat build with zero remote requests and deterministic output SHA-256.

title: 1. Audit current Rust dependency resolution against Gradle semantics
description: Establish the real current state of Rust dependency resolution and transport. Compare code, tests, corpus manifests, demo scripts, and PARITY claims. Identify what is truly native, what is shadow-only, what is JVM-owned, and what is partially verified.
acceptance_criteria: Produces a Beads note and, if needed, doc patch listing: supported dependency features; partially verified features; unsupported/fail-closed features; exact tests/corpus projects covering each claim; missing evidence. Must explicitly answer whether network fetch for Maven metadata/artifacts is Rust-owned, whether conflict resolution is Rust-owned, and whether Gradle can repeat a warm build with Rust avoiding remote requests.
notes:
Do not infer from architecture docs. Inspect executable code and rerun/inspect current demos. Any feature without direct test/corpus evidence must be marked partially verified or unsupported.
Detailed audit checklist:
- Inspect Rust substrate crates and JVM bridge code for dependency-related ownership boundaries.
- Identify whether Maven/Ivy metadata download is implemented in Rust, shadowed by Rust, or still JVM-owned.
- Identify whether artifact download, checksum verification, artifact store writes, and warm-cache reuse are Rust-owned.
- Identify whether version conflict selection, constraints, platforms/BOMs, variants/capabilities, exclusions, substitutions, and metadata rules are Rust-owned, JVM-owned, or unsupported.
- Inspect existing corpus manifests and runner assertions instead of trusting PARITY prose.
- Produce a Beads note with a table: feature, current owner, evidence path, risk, recommended next action.
- Open follow-up bugs immediately if code behavior contradicts PARITY or demo docs.
Forbidden shortcut: do not label a feature native just because Rust has a data model for it. It must execute on a checked-in project with no fallback.
AUDIT COMPLETE: 10/18 supported (POM parsing, version conflict, BOM, exclusions, dynamic versions, classifiers, artifact/metadata caching, checksums, SNAPSHOT resolution), 6/18 partially verified (module metadata no GMM parser, constraints Gradle block not parsed, rich versions missing strictly/reject, repo types Maven only, auth Basic only, prefetch SNAPSHOT fails closed), 4/18 unsupported (Ivy XML, dependency substitution, capabilities/variants, rich version keywords). Network fetch IS Rust-owned with cold/warm/no-network proof. Corpus has only 2 external projects - needs version conflict, transitive chain, BOM, dynamic version, multi-repo, SNAPSHOT coverage.
close_reason: Audit complete: dependency_resolution.rs (7249 LOC, 104 tests). SUPPORTED(10): POM parsing with parent/depMgmt/props, version conflict mediation (5 strategies), BOM imports, exclusions, dynamic versions+SNAPSHOT, classifiers/extensions, artifact caching (warm/cold/eviction), metadata caching, checksum verification (SHA-256/SHA-1/MD5), SNAPSHOT resolution. PARTIALLY VERIFIED(6): module metadata (no GMM parser), dependency constraints (Maven depMgmt works, Gradle constraints block not parsed), rich versions (missing strictly/reject), repo types (Maven only), auth (Basic only), prefetch (SNAPSHOT fails closed). UNSUPPORTED(4): Ivy XML, dependency substitution, capabilities/variants, rich version keywords. Network fetch IS Rust-owned for enabled builds. Corpus gaps: only 2 external projects, needs version conflict/transitive/BOM/dynamic/multi-repo/SNAPSHOT coverage.

title: Native dependency resolution hardening and first-60s demo
description: Make the next Rust substrate slice visible in the first 60 seconds of real use. Rust should own dependency metadata/artifact transport and cache behavior for native-ready builds, prove warm-cache/no-network wins, and keep authoritative DAG execution honest. This epic is intentionally evidence-driven: no claim is complete unless it is backed by checked-in corpus projects, reproducible runner output, parity assertions, and documentation updates.
acceptance_criteria: A reviewer can run one documented demo command and see Rust dependency fetch/cache behavior, Rust DAG authoritative execution, no JVM task forwarding for native-ready builds, and measurable first-60s improvements. Supported and external corpora pass with no fallback; unsupported dependency and task shapes fail closed with diagnostics; PARITY/demo docs and Beads notes include exact commands and result summaries.
notes:
Anti-shortcut rules: do not count synthetic microbenchmarks as parity; do not claim dependency solver parity without real Gradle corpus comparison; do not silently approximate dynamic versions, rich versions, substitutions, capabilities, or metadata rules; do not broaden native-ready mode unless unsupported cases are explicitly gated; do not update docs before runner evidence exists; do not hide JVM fallback behind success metrics.
Execution model for this epic:

Start means truth audit first. Do not implement or claim dependency resolution wins until gradle-fork-sh7.1 records what the code actually owns today and what evidence exists. Middle means build the evidence harness: real external dependency corpus, graph parity, cache/transport measurements, and fail-closed unsupported cases. End means one-command demo, docs updated from recorded artifacts only, and final ship-readiness review.

Global invariants:
- Rust authoritative execution must never silently fall back and still count as success.
- Native-ready expansion must be contract-gated and fail closed when Gradle semantics cannot be represented.
- Dependency-resolution claims must distinguish transport/cache/metadata parsing from full Gradle solver semantics.
- Any unsupported feature must have either a checked-in unsupported corpus test or a documented reason it cannot yet be exercised.
- Every performance claim must include command, machine-independent metric definition, result path, and comparison target.
- Every parity claim must compare upstream Gradle behavior against Rust authoritative behavior on the same checked-in project.
- No docs should say a feature is native unless the runner has a committed assertion for that feature.
close_reason: sh7 complete after verification hardening. Commit 0995368af1b8 landed the corrected dependency hardening slice; all reopened blockers closed with evidence; final gate sh7.9 closed. The slice is showable as Rust dependency transport/cache/read-through plus Rust authoritative DAG demo with declared dependency graph parity, not full Gradle solver parity.

description:
The scaffold is complete (33 services, 560 Rust tests, 27 shadow adapters, 261 Java tests). This epic covers the remaining work to make Gradle actually run builds through Rust.

## Strategy
Rather than replacing Gradle's subsystems wholesale (which would take years), we take an incremental approach:
1. Cut over already-validated subsystems to authoritative mode
2. Enhance Rust services to handle real workloads
3. Add Rust-native task execution for simple task types
4. Gather differential testing data from real builds

- Wave 1 (safety): Authoritative cut-over + differential testing
- Wave 2 (enhancement): Dependency resolution, toolchain, incremental compilation
- Wave 3 (execution): Rust-native task execution for simple tasks
- Wave 4 (optimization): Parallel execution, caching, build caching

title: Phase 5: Real JVM compatibility task execution
description:
Why this issue exists and what needs to be done:
RunBuild no longer silently succeeds when a task has no native executor, but the explicit JVM compatibility path is still a placeholder. Replace opt-in JVM_FORWARD bookkeeping with a real sidecar/worker execution contract, result reporting, failure propagation, and tests that distinguish executed JVM work from unsupported fallback.

Start:
Define the Rust↔JVM task execution contract and make placeholder forwarding impossible to mistake for executed work.

Middle:
Wire the sidecar/worker lifecycle and response handling so explicit JVM compatibility tasks return real success/failure/output metadata.

End:
A build containing legacy JVM tasks either executes them through the compatibility host or fails with a precise unsupported-task error; no noop fallback can report success.
acceptance_criteria: Explicit JVM compatibility execution has a protocol-level request/response, Rust records real outcomes from the sidecar/worker path, unsupported tasks fail precisely, and validation covers native-only, JVM-compat, and unsupported-task cases.
notes: Fixed Rust RunBuild accounting for the real Java execution mode. tasks_forwarded_to_jvm now counts jvm_gradle_task_executer / jvm_* execution modes, and tasks_skipped counts SKIPPED outcomes instead of the removed JVM_FORWARD placeholder. Added DAG regression test test_run_build_counts_gradle_engine_jvm_execution_mode. Validation: cargo test -p gradle-substrate-daemon server::dag_executor::tests passed; ./tools/stabilization/run_strict_stabilization.sh quick passed.
close_reason: Completed Phase 5 JVM compatibility task execution: Rust RunBuild now calls the JVM host over ExecuteTask, missing native executors fail unless explicit JVM forwarding is enabled, Java host execution requires Gradle's task engine rather than public-action fallback, unsupported cases return precise failures, and Rust accounting records jvm_gradle_task_executer as forwarded JVM work. title: Make Gradle Rust port production-grade
description:
Why this issue exists and what needs to be done:
The current fork has the right kernel/compatibility direction, but it is still prototype-shaped. The work needs to move from a promising mixed Rust/JVM experiment to a trustworthy Gradle substrate with honest contracts, stronger parity discipline, and a clearer path from shadow mode to authoritative mode.

Start:
Stabilize and simplify the Rust/JVM boundary so the repository tells the truth about what is authoritative, what is shadow-only, and what is still incomplete.

Middle:
Expand the canonical build-plan IR and JVM host so configuration misses can hand a real execution contract to Rust, then retire major bridge exclusions and improve lifecycle behavior.

End:
Reach a state where the mixed-mode port is measurably better: synchronized protocols, stronger compile/test gates, more realistic build-plan capture, fewer hidden fallbacks, and reliable differential validation against Gradle behavior.
design: Rust owns the hot path and durable state. JVM remains the compatibility island for DSL/plugin semantics until the IR is rich enough to carry real execution contracts. Keep upstream module names and boundaries recognizable.

title: Rust-native Java compilation via javac process
description:
Implement Java compilation task execution in Rust by spawning javac as a child process.

## What to do
1. Create JavaCompileExecutor that:

   - Constructs javac command line (source path, classpath, output dir, processor path)

2. Add classpath construction from resolved dependencies

4. Add incremental compilation integration (only compile changed files)

## Why this approach
We don't need to reimplement javac in Rust. We just need to ORCHESTRATE the javac process
more efficiently than Gradle's JVM-based execution does.

## Key advantage
Rust can manage the javac process lifecycle, parallel compilation of modules,
and classpath construction without JVM overhead.
